# Comparative Analysis of T1D Serious Games

Different game structures practise different skills. This chapter compares interaction patterns in games for ==type 1 diabetes (T1D)==; product facts and study results are collected in the [catalogue](../../explorer.html). The following design contrasts are interpretations, not measured head-to-head advantages.

## Design-archetype comparison

### Micro-puzzles versus broad simulation

[Level One](../../explorer.html#game-level-one) uses short, constrained problems, whereas [FlightGlucose](../../explorer.html#game-flightglucose) and [T1D Simulator](../../explorer.html#game-t1d-simulator) expose broader scenario systems. The micro-puzzle structure reduces the number of active variables and can make progression legible. A broad simulation can support interaction between factors and counterfactual comparison, but only if the learner can attribute a change to the relevant mechanisms.

**Design inference.** These approaches are complementary rather than mutually exclusive. Broad simulations may benefit from a micro-level entry sequence in which only one relation is actionable. Microgames may benefit from later transfer tasks that combine previously isolated relations. Comparative studies should test unfamiliar scenarios, not merely completion of each product's own levels.

### Care narrative versus system manipulation

[Rufus](../../explorer.html#game-rufus), [GlucoZor](../../explorer.html#game-glucozor) and [MyDiabetic](../../explorer.html#game-mydiabetic) organise learning around character care or everyday routines. Level One, FlightGlucose, and T1D Simulator place greater emphasis on manipulating variables and interpreting consequences, although their scope and degree of abstraction differ.

Narrative and character identification can support attention, emotional distance, and discussion, but a character is not a mechanism by itself. [Nørlev et al. (2022)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34024156/) identified narrative, feedback, goals, avatars, simulation, levels, and social interaction across T1D games, but the review could not establish an optimal combination.

**Design inference.** Character-based context is most educationally useful when it changes the reasoning problem: for example, when the scenario makes time, uncertainty, competing goals, or caregiver roles visible. Cosmetic narrative without integration into decisions may improve presentation without improving transfer.

### Procedural rehearsal versus causal explanation

MyDiabetic and Rufus foreground care tasks. Level One, FlightGlucose, and T1D Simulator foreground causal consequences to different degrees. Historical Koodak-e-Tavana work illustrates the value of a narrowly specified procedural target: a 30-child randomised study reported reduced insulin-injection distress over one week, but its size and follow-up constrain generalisation ([Ebrahimpour et al., 2015](https://doi.org/10.5812/ijp.25(3)2015.427)).

**Comparative implication.** A procedural game should measure procedure performance or procedure-related distress. A causal simulation should measure prediction, explanation, and transfer. Neither should borrow the other's evidence simply because both concern T1D.

## What participatory research adds

MyDiabetic and the Nørlev smartphone prototype document participatory work with children or families ([Novak, 2024](https://doi.org/10.2196/49478); [Nørlev et al., 2022](https://doi.org/10.2196/33955)). Other products document varying combinations of clinical, academic, commercial, nonprofit, or lived-experience involvement, but public descriptions rarely establish who controlled learning objectives, physiological claims, interaction decisions, or long-term maintenance.

Lived experience and participatory co-design answer related but different questions. Lived experience can identify neglected problems and sustain motivation. Participatory methods can reveal variation between intended users and make design decisions auditable. Neither replaces physiological validation or outcome evaluation.

## Priority comparative studies

1. Compare a micro-puzzle introduction with a broad-simulation introduction on time to meaningful action, comprehension, and dropout.
2. Compare static explanation, worked animation, and interactive counterfactual replay on delayed transfer to unseen glucose scenarios.
3. Test whether character-based context improves explanation, memory, distress, or caregiver discussion, and identify for whom it does not.
4. Separate effects in children, adolescents, newly diagnosed adults, experienced adults, and caregivers.
5. Archive the exact intervention version, assessment, tutorial state, and scenario set so a later product update does not inherit unsupported evidence.
6. Report adverse interpretations, including false confidence, model over-trust, shame, anxiety, and unsafe real-world experimentation.

## Abbreviation glossary

**T1D - Type 1 diabetes.** An autoimmune disease requiring exogenous insulin because insulin-producing beta cells are destroyed.
